::: {#rem-collision-entropy}
#### The expected probability is the collision probability

[Entropy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-entropy) is the [expectation](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-expectation) of the [surprisal](#def-surprisal) $-\log \P(X)$.
Taking the expectation of the [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $\P(X)$ itself summarizes $X$ differently.
For a [discrete random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-discrete-rv) $X$, let $X'$ be an [independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-independence) copy of $X$.
Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{\P(X)}
&= \sum_x \P(X=x)^2 \\
&= \P(X = X').
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the collision probability, the chance that two independent draws agree.
For a [continuous random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-continuous-rv) with [density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf) $\p$, the analogue is $\E{\p(X)} = \int \p(x)^2\,dx$,
which the [expected-density exercise](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#exr-expected-density) computes
for the uniform and [normal distributions](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-normal).

The Rényi entropy of order 2, also called the collision entropy, is the negative [logarithm](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm) of this quantity <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
[@wikipedia_renyi_entropy]:

$$H_2(X) = -\log \E{\P(X)}.$$

It is at most the [Shannon entropy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-entropy) $\entropyf{X} = \E{-\log \P(X)}$,
because $-\log$ is a [convex function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-sums.html#def-convex-function) and Jensen's inequality gives $\E{-\log \P(X)} \ge -\log \E{\P(X)}$. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
The two coincide when $X$ is uniform,
since then $\P(X)$ takes the same value for every value of $X$.

:::
